lead: This unit explains how quantum mechanics changes secret-key distribution, information compression and error correction. You will learn BB84 and E91, the Shannon and Schumacher limits, classical and quantum codes, and the ideas behind fault-tolerant quantum computers. After it you can compute sifted keys, entropy limits and simple code syndromes, and explain why scalable quantum computing needs error correction.
about: Unit 5 shows how information behaves when the carrier is a quantum state. Chapter 5.1 sets up private-key cryptography and the key-distribution problem. Chapter 5.2 solves that problem with BB84 and E91. Chapter 5.3 compares classical and quantum information, then 5.4 and 5.5 give the noiseless and noisy coding limits. Chapter 5.6 teaches classical error-correcting codes, which supply the distance and syndrome ideas for the three- and nine-qubit codes in 5.7. Chapter 5.8 explains why encoded qubits need fault-tolerant gates for a scalable quantum computer.

chapters.idea: Private-key cryptography hides messages behind a shared secret key, but distributing that key securely is the weak point.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a full topic, so keep it short. Cover the private-key model: plaintext m, ciphertext c, shared key k, encryption c=E_k(m), decryption m=D_k(c). Define perfect secrecy, one-time pad c=m⊕k (⊕ is bitwise XOR), block ciphers DES and AES, and the key-distribution problem. Mention public-key ideas (RSA, Diffie–Hellman) only as contrast. Some syllabi call the one-time pad the Vernam cipher.

figure.title: Private-key encryption
figure.aria: Plaintext is encrypted with a shared secret key into ciphertext and decrypted with the same key.

chapters.example: Alice and Bob share the 4-bit one-time pad key k=0110. Alice sends message m=1011. Compute c=m⊕k and show Bob recovers m. Answer: c=1011⊕0110=1101. Bob computes c⊕k=1101⊕0110=1011, so m is recovered.
chapters.trap: The one-time-pad key must be random, as long as the message, and used only once. Reusing a key leaks m₁⊕m₂ and breaks perfect secrecy.
chapters.prereq: None beyond basic probability and binary arithmetic.
chapters.leave: Public-key mathematics and quantum key distribution go to 5.2.

chapters.idea: Quantum key distribution lets two users detect eavesdropping because measuring an unknown quantum state disturbs it.
chapters.depth: Cover BB84 in full: four states |0>, |1>, |+>, |−>, two bases + and ×, sifting, error estimation, privacy amplification. Cover E91 with entangled pairs and a Bell/CHSH test. Use names: BB84 is the four-state protocol; E91 is entanglement-based QKD. Keep security proof at idea level: no-cloning and disturbance.

figure.aria: Alice sends four qubits; Bob announces measurement bases; only positions with matching bases form the sifted key.

chapters.example: Alice sends four BB84 qubits: (bit 0, basis +), (bit 1, basis +), (bit 1, basis ×), (bit 0, basis ×). Bob measures in bases +, ×, ×, +. Which positions survive sifting and what is the sifted key? Answer: positions 1 and 3 match. Alice's bits there are 0 and 1, so the sifted key is 01.
chapters.trap: After sifting, Alice and Bob compare only a sample of bits to estimate the error rate; they do not announce the whole key. Also, an eavesdropper cannot copy an unknown qubit because of the no-cloning theorem.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 measurement and Bell states; Unit 3 no-cloning theorem.
chapters.leave: Security proofs and device-independent QKD are beyond this unit.

chapters.idea: Classical information uses bits and Shannon entropy; quantum information uses qubits and von Neumann entropy, with extra constraints such as no-cloning and disturbance.
chapters.depth: Compare bit versus qubit, Shannon entropy H(X)=−Σ p log₂ p and von Neumann entropy S(ρ)=−Tr(ρ log₂ ρ). Define density matrix ρ, mixed state, mutual information, Holevo bound as an accessible-information limit. Some syllabi say 'classical information theory versus quantum information theory'. Keep proofs out; use two-level examples.

figure.aria: Classical probability vectors form a subset of quantum density matrices.

chapters.example: A fair coin has H=1 bit. A qubit in state |+> has S=1 bit. For p=0.9, H₂(0.9)=−0.9 log₂0.9−0.1 log₂0.1≈0.469 bits; the diagonal density matrix ρ=diag(0.9,0.1) also has S(ρ)≈0.469 bits.
chapters.trap: A qubit's state has continuous parameters, but the Holevo bound limits accessible classical information to at most 1 bit per qubit for a single qubit. Do not say one qubit stores two classical bits.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 density operators and measurement; basic logarithms.
chapters.leave: Compression theorems go to 5.4; noisy channel capacity goes to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Entropy gives the ultimate compression limit: Shannon entropy for classical data and von Neumann entropy for quantum data.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. State Shannon's noiseless channel coding theorem: a source with entropy H(X) compresses to about H(X) bits per symbol as n→∞. State Schumacher's theorem: n copies of ρ compress to about nS(ρ) qubits with fidelity →1. Define typical sequence and typical subspace. Mention 'quantum noiseless coding theorem' as another name. No proof.

figure.title: Schumacher compression
figure.aria: Many copies of a quantum state are compressed into the typical subspace, stored in about nS(ρ) qubits, then decompressed.

chapters.example: A source emits copies of ρ with eigenvalues 0.9 and 0.1. Then S(ρ)=−0.9 log₂0.9−0.1 log₂0.1≈0.469 qubits per copy. For n=1000 copies, Schumacher compression uses about nS(ρ)≈469 qubits with fidelity close to 1.
chapters.trap: Compression needs many identical copies. A single unknown qubit cannot be compressed or cloned, and the theorem is asymptotic in n.
chapters.leave: Noisy channels and capacity go to 5.5; quantum error correction goes to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A noisy quantum channel carries classical messages at a rate limited by the Holevo quantity and related capacities.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Model a noisy quantum channel N, an encoder, a decoder and classical messages X,Y. Define the Holevo quantity χ and the Holevo bound; state that classical capacity is bounded by χ and that entangled inputs can need regularization. Use bit-flip and depolarizing channels as examples. Some syllabi call this 'classical capacity of a quantum channel'.

figure.title: Classical messages over a quantum channel
figure.aria: A classical message is encoded into quantum states, sent through a noisy quantum channel, and decoded into a classical message.

chapters.example: A bit-flip channel flips the input bit with probability p=0.1. Its classical capacity for this simple input is C=1−H₂(0.1), where H₂(p)=−p log₂p−(1−p)log₂(1−p). Since H₂(0.1)≈0.469, C≈0.531 bits per channel use.
chapters.trap: The Holevo bound limits accessible information from one use of an ensemble. It is not always the full capacity when entangled inputs across many channel uses are allowed.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 Shannon and von Neumann entropy; 5.4 coding limits.
chapters.leave: Quantum error-correcting codes go to 5.7; fault tolerance goes to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Classical error correction adds redundancy so that errors can be detected or corrected by looking at a syndrome.
chapters.depth: Cover repetition code, Hamming distance d, minimum distance d_min, error detection/correction t=⌊(d_min−1)/2⌋. Explain linear codes, generator matrix G, parity-check matrix H, syndrome decoding. Work Hamming(7,4) at block level. Some syllabi call these 'classical error-correcting codes' or 'block codes'.

figure.title: Repetition code, rate 1/3
figure.aria: Each message bit is repeated three times; majority vote corrects the flipped bit in the first block.

chapters.example: Message 101 is encoded by a 3-bit repetition code as 111 000 111. The received word is 101 000 111, so one bit in the first block flipped. Majority vote on each block gives 1, 0, 1, so the decoded message is 101.
chapters.trap: A distance-3 code corrects one error, not two. If two bits flip in the same block, majority vote gives the wrong bit.
chapters.leave: Quantum codes and syndrome measurement go to 5.7.

chapters.idea: Quantum error correction encodes one logical qubit into entangled physical qubits and measures a syndrome without measuring the encoded information.
chapters.depth: Cover the three-qubit bit-flip code, the three-qubit phase-flip code, and the nine-qubit Shor code. Define logical states |0_L>, |1_L>, syndrome measurement and recovery. Explain why direct measurement of data qubits is forbidden. Some syllabi call this 'quantum error-correcting codes' and the nine-qubit code the Shor code.

figure.title: Three-qubit bit-flip code
figure.aria: A logical qubit is encoded into three physical qubits, a bit flip is located by a syndrome, and the flip is corrected.

chapters.example: Encode |ψ>=α|0>+β|1> as α|000>+β|111>. A bit flip on qubit 2 gives α|010>+β|101>. The syndrome shows qubit 2 differs from qubits 1 and 3. Apply X to qubit 2 and recover α|000>+β|111>.
chapters.trap: Do not measure the three data qubits in the computational basis to find the error; that destroys α and β. Measure only parity or syndrome information.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 classical codes; Unit 2 measurement; Unit 3 CNOT and Pauli gates.
chapters.leave: Fault-tolerant gates and thresholds go to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Fault-tolerant quantum computation performs gates and measurements on encoded qubits so that one physical fault does not become a logical error.
chapters.depth: Cover fault-tolerant gates, transversal gates, syndrome extraction with ancilla qubits, concatenation and the threshold theorem. Explain error propagation and why fault tolerance is more than QEC. Mention magic-state distillation only by name. Some syllabi call this 'fault-tolerant quantum computation'.

figure.title: Fault-tolerant logical gate
figure.aria: Logical qubits are encoded, a transversal gate acts, ancillas help extract the syndrome, and errors are corrected before the logical output.

chapters.example: A logical gate uses three physical gates, each failing with probability p=0.001. The logical gate fails only if two or more physical gates fail. Probability ≈ C(3,2)p²(1−p)+p³ = 3(0.001)²(0.999)+(0.001)³ ≈ 3×10⁻⁶.
chapters.trap: Fault tolerance is not just adding a quantum error-correcting code. A single fault must not spread to two faults inside a logical gate, and the physical error rate must be below a threshold.
chapters.prereq: 5.7 quantum error-correcting codes; Unit 3 universal gates.
chapters.leave: Surface codes and detailed threshold calculations are beyond this unit.
